strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing gap between academic benchmarks and real-world deployment; clearly identifies that existing detectors fail on cross-forgery and cross-domain scenarios
Comprehensive HydraFake-100K dataset with hierarchical evaluation protocol, diverse forgery types, quality control procedures, and inclusion of social media/commercial data
Strong empirical results with 90.7% average accuracy, substantial gains on cross-forgery (+8.1%) and cross-domain (+15.1%), and superior reasoning quality vs general-purpose MLLMs
Thorough experimental validation including extensive ablations isolating each component's contribution, multiple base model comparisons, and robustness evaluation
Good reproducibility with detailed appendix providing prompts, procedures, and promise to release dataset

Critical failure on low-resolution images (e.g., 58.6% on DeepFaceLab); authors acknowledge MLLMs excel at 512×512+ but fail at low-res, severely limiting practical deployment without proposed solutions

Evaluation limitations: cross-domain split still uses primarily high-resolution in-domain real images; social media data limited (1-2K); no cross-dataset evaluation; Effort baseline significantly outperforms on face relighting (94.8% vs 75.7%)

strengths: Significant dataset contribution addressing real gap in benchmarks—HydraFake's hierarchical evaluation protocol (in-domain, cross-model, cross-forgery, cross-domain) is well-motivated and will be valuable long-term resource
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including 10 SOTA detectors, 6 MLLMs, cross-benchmark validation, extensive ablations, and reasoning quality assessment via both score-based and pairwise methods

Strong empirical results with 6.0% average improvement over prior SOTA and particularly notable gains on cross-forgery (+6.2%) and cross-domain (+3.3%) scenarios, with generalization demonstrated across multiple benchmarks (LOKI, FakeClue, AIGIBench)

Well-motivated pattern-aware reasoning grounded in human forensic processes, with clear intuitive framework and sophisticated two-stage training pipeline combining cold-start (SFT + MiPO) and reinforcement learning
Excellent reproducibility and transparency with detailed prompt templates, annotation pipelines, implementation details, hyperparameters, and honest failure case analysis

Practical insights demonstrating MLLM advantages on high-resolution images while identifying low-resolution limitations, and showing reasoning can provide interpretability without sacrificing accuracy
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components—pattern-aware reasoning is structured CoT adapted for deepfakes, SFT + preference optimization is standard LLM fine-tuning, and GRPO adaptation is straightforward; core novelty lies in combination rather than fundamental techniques

Evaluation limitations: training protocol uses only 3 of 21 forgery types (unrealistic), predominantly high-resolution modern generators (2024-2025) with limited older deepfakes, performance gap between scenarios (98.6% cross-model vs 82.2% cross-domain) suggests scenario-dependent robustness, and unfair zero-shot vs fine-tuned MLLM comparisons

Generalization claims overclaimed given low-resolution failure cases, limited video evaluation by design, domain bias toward high-res modern generators, and cold-start model 3-5% accuracy drop suggesting data-dependent learning

Methodological concerns: reward design (Eq. 5-6) appears ad-hoc with no sensitivity analysis, pattern selection not fully justified with limited ablation of combinations, MiPO design rationale weak (why this specific mix of s_ℓ^φ and s_ℓ^ψ?), reflection reward adds external model dependency, hyperparameter choices (β=0, β'=0) disable KL penalties without ablation

Practical deployment challenges not addressed: 49.76s inference cost per batch vs milliseconds for CNNs, model brittleness evident from cold-start performance gap, unclear adaptation mechanism for emerging forgery techniques, no computational/latency trade-off analysis
Dataset release timeline and commercial app licensing status unclear, potentially limiting reproducibility and adoption; licensing of GPT-4o/Dreamina data for training may create restrictions

strengths: Comprehensive hierarchical evaluation protocol addressing real gap between existing benchmarks and industrial practice
Carefully constructed HydraFake dataset with modern forgery types, quality control, and in-the-wild social media data
Extensive experimental evaluation with thorough ablations, cross-benchmark validation, and comparison with 20+ baselines
Strong empirical results with notable improvements on cross-forgery (90.3%) and cross-domain (82.2%) scenarios
Transparent and interpretable reasoning-based outputs valuable for forensic applications
Reproducibility efforts including detailed implementation details and comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (SFT, DPO, GRPO) without fundamental algorithmic innovations; pattern-aware reasoning is intuitive but not principled

Arbitrary design choices: reward thresholds (2.0, 1.0, -0.5, -1.0) lack justification; pattern selection appears post-hoc; MiPO mixing strategy not explained

Serious generalization concerns: 58.6% accuracy on low-resolution DeepFaceLab severely limits deployment; cross-domain results primarily on high-resolution images; overstated claims about AIGC detection beyond facial forgeries
Evaluation protocol issues: new dataset evaluated with new method limits independent validation; VERITAS-MINI comparison artificial; no statistical significance testing

Incomplete technical analysis: missing ablations (MiPO vs standard DPO, reward sensitivity), no adversarial robustness testing, limited failure analysis, inference overhead not thoroughly addressed

strengths: Comprehensive HydraFake dataset with rigorous hierarchical evaluation protocol (in-domain, cross-model, cross-forgery, cross-domain) addressing realistic OOD scenarios—valuable benchmark contribution
Well-motivated pattern-aware reasoning framework grounded in human forensic analysis; two-stage training pipeline (SFT + MiPO + P-GRPO) is principled and technically sound
Strong empirical results: 90.7% average accuracy with significant improvements on cross-forgery (90.3%) and cross-domain (82.2%), outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Pro
Exceptional experimental rigor: comparisons with 18+ baselines, thorough ablations, cross-benchmark validation (LOKI, FakeClue, Forensics-Bench), robustness analysis, and reasoning quality evaluation
Transparent and reproducible: complete implementation details, prompts, qualitative examples, and failure cases provided; cold-start model serves as useful reasoning foundation
Mixed Preference Optimization (MiPO) cleverly addresses limited preference data by mixing different error types; P-GRPO with pattern-aware rewards enables adaptive reasoning
weaknesses: Limited method novelty: combines established techniques (SFT, MiPO, GRPO/DPO) with primary contribution being application-specific prompt engineering; pattern-aware reasoning is well-motivated but intuitive (Table 2 shows modest 6.2% improvement over flexible reasoning)

Theoretical gaps: no explanation for why reasoning helps cross-forgery generalization more than cross-model; unclear whether improvements stem from better features or increased supervision; connection between patterns and OOD robustness remains empirical

Evaluation limitations: 'fair comparison' constraints for MLLM baselines feel artificial; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; weak low-resolution performance (DeepFaceLab 58.6%) unresolved; only 1K in-the-wild real images limits robustness claims

Technical design choices lack justification: P-GRPO reward values (2.0, 1.0, -0.5, -1.0) appear heuristic; pattern detection mechanism (P, R flags) undefined; non-preference data mixing in MiPO not ablated

Scope limitations: restricted to static facial images; video/audio/multimodal deepfakes not addressed; applicability to other domains unclear; method dependence on large LLMs limits practical deployment
